parts.title: My Saturdays at the care home
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was thirteen, my mother suggested that I should do some volunteer work. I was not keen. I imagined myself doing boring jobs for people who would not even say thank you. However, my mother had already phoned the local care home, and the next Saturday I was standing in front of the door with a bunch of flowers I had bought, because I did not know what else to bring.

The manager, a cheerful woman called Mrs Adeyemi, took me to the lounge, where about ten residents were drinking tea. She asked me to talk to Mr Bellamy, who sat alone by the window. I was nervous, and my first question was stupid: I asked him if he was bored. He looked at me for a moment, and then he laughed. He told me that he had been a ship's cook for thirty years and had visited forty countries.

After that, I went every Saturday. Mr Bellamy taught me to make a perfect omelette, and in return, I taught him to send photos on his phone. One day, his niece wrote to him from Canada, and he was so happy that he showed the message to everyone in the room.

Last month, Mr Bellamy died, at the age of ninety-one. His family asked me to speak at the funeral, and I said that he had taught me more than any teacher. I am now training to help at a hospital, because I have learnt that listening to people is also a kind of help.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel about volunteering at first?
questions.explanation: She says she was not keen and imagined boring jobs.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer's first question surprise Mr Bellamy?
options: It was not a very polite question.
He had expected a longer speech.
He was not used to being asked anything.
questions.explanation: She asked him if he was bored, which was a stupid question; he looked at her and then laughed.

questions.prompt: What did the writer learn from Mr Bellamy?
options: How to cook a simple dish
questions.explanation: He taught her to make a perfect omelette.

questions.prompt: Why was Mr Bellamy happy one day?
options: He had a visit from a friend.
He won a prize at the home.
He received a message from a relative.
questions.explanation: His niece wrote to him from Canada and he showed the message to everyone.

questions.prompt: What is the writer doing now?
options: Writing a book about Mr Bellamy
Preparing to help in a hospital
questions.explanation: She is training to help at a hospital because she has learnt that listening is a kind of help.

parts.title: A moustache for charity
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every November, thousands of people in the UK take part in a charity challenge called Movember. [1] The name comes from "moustache" and "November", and the aim is to raise money for men's health.

The idea began in Australia about twenty years ago, when two friends decided to grow moustaches for a month. [2] They wanted to start a conversation about health problems that men often do not like to discuss.

Today, the challenge is one of the largest in the world. [3] Women can also take part by supporting the men in their lives, or by walking or running every day. Many companies encourage their staff to join in.

The money pays for research and for services such as telephone helplines. [4] Some of the people who call say that the helpline saved their lives.

For those who take part, it is also a chance to have fun. People send photos of their moustaches to friends, and offices play games. [5] As one volunteer says, "It started as a joke, but it became something serious."
sentences: Men start the month with a clean face and let their moustaches grow for thirty days.
The helplines are open all day and night, and anybody can call.
Millions of pounds have been raised since it began.
Doctors also advise men to visit them once a year.
They got a lot of attention, and people wanted to know why.
However, the competition also makes people think about serious problems.

gaps.explanation: "Movember" is introduced and then explained: men grow moustaches for thirty days; the next sentence explains the name.
The two friends grew moustaches; they got attention and people wanted to know why, so they wanted to start a conversation.
"One of the largest in the world" is supported by the fact that millions of pounds have been raised; the next sentence adds that women can join too.
The money pays for services such as helplines; the next sentence refers to the helplines being open day and night, and the callers.
"However" links the fun of competitions with the serious side; the volunteer's comment continues the contrast.

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing [1] ask about volunteering at your charity shop. I am sixteen years old, and I [2] free on Saturday mornings. I have worked [3] a waiter at my uncle's café for a year, so I am used to talking to people. I would be happy to help in any way [4] you need. Could you tell me [5] time I should come for an interview? I look forward [6] hearing from you.

gaps.explanation: "I am writing to ask" is the standard way to give the purpose of a letter.
"I am free" uses the verb be with the adjective free.
"Worked as a waiter" names the job.
The relative pronoun links "way" with "you need".
"What time" asks about the time of the interview.
"Look forward to" is followed by -ing; to is a preposition here.

turns.text: Hello, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Dorothea, and I'm organising this year's Fun Run for the children's hospital. parts.title: An interview with a soup kitchen manager
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Cuthbert, you manage a kitchen that gives free meals to people in need. How did it begin?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: Fifteen years ago, I was a chef in a hotel. One winter night, I saw a hungry man in the street, looking for food in a bin. That shocked me. The next day I started to take the leftovers to the people who slept near the station.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How many people come now?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: About a hundred and fifty every evening. We have a team of forty volunteers, and some of them used to be customers themselves.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the food come from?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: Mostly from supermarkets, which give us fruit and vegetables that are slightly damaged but perfectly good. Local restaurants also help, and farmers bring potatoes at harvest time.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the hardest part of the work?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: The cold. In winter, the queue is longer, and standing outside for an hour is hard for people. We are trying to find a bigger building with a waiting room.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you want people to understand?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: That anybody can end up in difficulty. A job loss, an illness, a family problem, and everything can change very quickly. The people who come here are not different from you or me.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How can people help?

turns.speaker: barnaby3
turns.text: Money helps, of course, but time is even more valuable. Even two hours a month makes a difference. And a smile and a kind word cost nothing.
